title: How train events are detected
summary: Each event is flagged by listening for a train horn, then confirmed by a human before it appears here. Only human-confirmed trains are shown, and clip audio is private by default.
method: A microphone about 1,500–1,700 ft from the freight line records the soundscape.

Software scans for a train horn — sustained, tonal energy in a narrow frequency band. A horn is close to a pure tone; wind, planes, and engines are broadband noise, so a 'tonality' ratio separates them.
A stretch of horn-like tone becomes a 'blast'; horn blasts close together (within a few minutes) are grouped into one train pass.
Every candidate is reviewed by a human — only confirmed trains are published. The recordings come from a backyard mic, so audio stays private unless a clip is individually published.

accuracy.note: Measured for the tuned horn detector against the labeled examples (clips within 5 minutes counted as one train pass). The human review is the final guarantee on what's shown.

caveats: Distance: only the horn carries this far, so a quiet pass with no horn won't be caught.
One backyard mic: no train direction or speed, and audio can catch nearby conversation — which is why clips stay private unless individually published.
Look-alikes: planes and sirens can sound horn-like; the human review is the safeguard.
Counts reflect horn events we caught and confirmed — not necessarily every train that passed.
The automatic detector is still being refined from each new batch of confirmed examples, so the parameters above evolve.
